entries.title: N.C. Republicans Pick State Lawmaker to Replace Chuck Edwards on Ballot
entries.summary: State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom will be the Republican nominee after Edwards dropped out over a sexual harassment scandal.
entries.content:
North Carolina Republican Party officials have selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot, after he withdrew from the race in the wake of a House Ethics Committee report that he sexually harassed two of his staffers.

The North Carolina Republican Party's 11th Congressional District Executive Committee met in a closed-door meeting Monday night to select between multiple candidates: Ken McKim, Chad Nesbitt, Matthew Burril, Kristie Sluder and Balkcom. According to North Carolina GOP rules, each member of the committee must vote for their preferred candidate, and whichever candidate gets over 50% of the vote first becomes the nominee.

Balkcom, who has served in the state’s House of Representatives since 2023, will face Democratic nominee Jamie Ager in November.

Last week, the House Ethics Committee recommended that Edwards be censured and found “substantial evidence” that the North Carolina Republican “violated the spirit of the House’s prohibition on sexual harassment and unwanted advances through his conduct” toward two female staffers in his office.

Edwards, the committee said in its report, “acknowledged” that his behavior “could be viewed as inappropriate.” He gave the staffers expensive jewelry, designer purses, vacations, guns and dinners.

In 2022, Edwards ousted a controversial Republican incumbent, Madison Cawthorn, and was viewed as a safer candidate to represent the district, which stretches across most of the western part of the state. But his own ethics issues have caused headaches for GOP leaders. Republicans in the House and the Senate had privately pushed Edwards to drop out from the race shortly after the ethics panel released its findings.

The race for North Carolina’s 11th District is one of two competitive House contests in the state. House Democrats’ campaign arm has been targeting the seat, with Ager being added to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” program in February.

entries.title: Ken Paxton’s Political Operation Rakes In Data Center Donations as Texans Turn Against Industry
entries.summary: The Republican Senate candidate has tried to avoid data center fights. His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has called for more regulations.
entries.content:
In February, Hood County, Texas, asked state Attorney General Ken Paxton if it had the authority to temporarily block data center development.

Almost six months later, Paxton, the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, still hasn’t weighed in. He’s remained relatively quiet on the data center issue, which he called “complicated” during an interview with Valuetainment released in May.

Meanwhile, Paxton has benefited from hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of data center industry money pouring into his political operation.

Paxton’s complicated and lucrative relationship with the data center industry is fast becoming a liability. Polls indicate that Texas voters are rebelling against data center construction, and his own poll numbers are sagging.

James Talarico, Paxton’s opponent, who is seeking to become the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since the early 1990s, has called for more regulations on data center development. This includes repealing Texas’ data center sales-tax exemption, something Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has also asked state lawmakers to take up.
James.Talarico (7994x5329, AR: 1.50)As lawmakers across the political spectrum talk about cracking down on data centers, industry PACs and executives have invested heavily in getting Paxton, who seems less inclined to do so, elected.

Neither the Paxton campaign nor the Texas attorney general's office responded to requests for comment from NOTUS.

Through June, Paxton’s federal political operation has received at least $448,000 from executives and political committees of companies building, operating and investing in data centers, according to a NOTUS review of Federal Election Commission reports filed by several related political committees — his campaign, leadership PAC, joint fundraising committees and a pro-Paxton super PAC called Lone Star Liberty PAC.

On June 30, SAGO Energy LP contributed $100,000 to Paxton Victory, a joint fundraising committee that splits the money it receives among Paxton’s Senate campaign and leadership PAC and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. SAGO Energy is owned by WTG Energy, which also provides energy for data centers — and may have run afoul of federal campaign finance law, which prohibits corporations from contributing to candidates.

Tyler Winklevoss, founder of Winklevoss Capital Management and the cryptocurrency exchange Gemini, also donated $13,500 to Paxton Victory on June 30. One of Winklevoss Capital’s portfolio companies, Crusoe Energy, provides data center infrastructure, and Winklevoss previously worked with a Dallas-based firm to develop gas-powered data centers.

CRH Americas Inc. PAC and Valero PAC also gave $5,000 each to Paxton’s campaign on June 30, according to the Paxton campaign’s July quarterly report. CRH, a building materials company, was working on more than 100 data center projects this spring, according to Yahoo Finance. Valero is best known for its fuel stations, but Valero Energy has a 25-acre data center outside San Antonio, according to Bloomberg.

The list goes on: At least 17 corporate PACs and executives that invest in, build or operate data centers have donated to Paxton’s political operation, according to NOTUS’s analysis of FEC data.

Paxton defeated longtime Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in an upset primary runoff victory in May.

But Paxton needs all the money he can get: While his Senate campaign had raised more than $9.2 million as of June 30, it entered the summer campaign stretch with almost $1.8 million in cash on hand, according to the latest report to the FEC.

That’s significantly less than the Talarico campaign, which had more than $21.5 million in cash on hand as of June 30, according to its latest FEC report.

The Texas Senate race leans Republican, according to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, but recent polling has found Talarico with a slight lead.

“Paxton is in the fight of his life,” Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller told NOTUS. When asked about the political liability of accepting donations from the data center industry while keeping out of the policy fray, said Paxton was likely “trying to stay out of controversy.”
Sid.Miller (5056x3564, AR: 1.42)But, he added, Republicans overall “need to get right on the issue and defend the people's position, or they're likely to get beat.”

Talarico’s political operation has arguably benefitted from data center industry interests, including a $10 million donation to the pro-Talarico super PAC Lone Star Rising from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who has invested in and advocates for the role of data centers in providing much-needed computing power. But unlike Paxton, Talarico has presented a platform for regulating data centers.

The issue of whether to facilitate the creation of data centers — facilities filled with equipment to store, process and send data across networks, enabling people to stream shows, query artificial intelligence platforms or tap a card at checkout — have emerged as a flash point in the state, and across the country.

Concerns that these power-hungry sites will increase electricity prices, divert water resources, pollute the environment and disrupt communities with widely cited noise, including from backup generators, have prompted public backlash that’s had data center developers and operators on the backfoot.

The Texas Tribune identified at least 335 data centers operating in Texas — the second highest number after Virginia — with at least 248 planned to arrive in the coming years. By 2030, Texas is projected to have the largest data center market in the world, according to the real estate advisory firm JLL.
Data.Center.Texas (4061x2284, AR: 1.78)Even when Texas communities push back on data center construction, there is little recourse. The Texas Tribune also reported that after a data center developer sued Hill County, Texas, in May for trying to impose a moratorium after community backlash, the county instead implemented a list of requirements for data center developers.

During Paxton’s interview with Valuetainment, which was published May 15, he framed the data center issue as a competition with China that the United States “cannot lose.”

“On the other hand, I have a lot of sensitivity to local communities that don’t want things built next to their neighborhoods,” Paxton added. “There’s always going to be tension between development and local needs, and I think that needs to be decided by local communities, potentially with the input of their state officials.”

In February, Hood County asked Paxton — in his capacity as attorney general — to decide whether the county has the authority to impose a moratorium on data center development.

As of Monday, the request is still “pending,” according to the attorney general’s website.

Meanwhile, data center donations to Paxton’s political team keep coming.

A few individual donors with ties to the data center industry made donations to Paxton’s campaign last fall.

Last November, Laurie Harrison, executive director of the Rosewood Corporation, donated $7,000 to Paxton’s campaign. One of Rosewood’s portfolio companies, General Informatics, owns at least three data centers.

In October 2025, Paxton’s campaign also reported receiving $7,000 each from David Capobianco, CEO of the private equity firm Five Point Infrastructure, which has moved into data center development, and his wife, Rosangela Capobianco. Albert Huddleston, managing partner at Aethon Energy, which announced a data center development partnership with Mitsubishi earlier this year, also gave $7,000 to Paxton’s campaign.

And the month before that, Paxton’s campaign received $2,000 from Farzad Vahid, CEO of data center supplier Fornida, and $2,500 from “C.M. Yokubaitis,” CEO of Data Foundry, which owns several data centers in Texas. “C.M.” appears to be co-CEO Carolyn Yokubaitis.

But donations exploded this spring as public sentiment soured on data centers.

Harrison contributed $100,000 to Paxton Victory on June 22, according to the joint fundraising committee’s latest report to the FEC. Huddleston chipped in another $3,500 to another joint fundraising committee, Team Paxton, at the end of June.

On June 26, Charles “Bubba” Saulsbury Jr. of Saulsbury Industries gave $100,000 to Paxton Victory. The company provides a range of engineering, construction and procurement services for data center development, according to its website, and Saulsbury himself is a prominent MAGA donor.

And on June 15, Todd Platt, CEO of Hillwood, a Texas-based real estate development company, donated $3,500 to Paxton’s campaign. Hillwood has been working on data centers for more than two decades, according to its website, and developed a 400-acre data center north of Fort Worth.

In May, the Ken Paxton Victory Fund, another joint fundraising committee that splits money between Paxton’s campaign and leadership PAC and Lone Star Liberty PAC, reported receiving $17,000 from Seth Crawford, vice president of land at Black Mountain Energy Storage, which is developing a data center near Forth Worth. Jason Les, CEO of data center developer and operator Riot Platforms, chipped in $1,000.

The committee also reported receiving $10,000 from Javier Loya, founder of GetChoice!, a utility management consultant for data centers, and $7,000 from John Durham, CEO of JV Industrial Companies, which operates a data center in La Porte, Texas.

On May 19, William Kent, CEO of the Kent Companies, gave $50,000 to Lone Star Liberty PAC. Kent Companies is a data center construction company operating in Texas and across the United States, according to its website.

None of the donors or companies immediately responded to NOTUS’ requests for comment on their contributions to Paxton’s political operation.

entries.title: After a Year in D.C., the National Guard Seems Almost Normal
entries.summary: Critics say that's exactly the problem.
entries.content:
On a recent Saturday, Starburst Plaza was something it’s often not: quiet.

A few people sat on benches on the triangular plot that stands at the five-way intersection of H Street, Florida Avenue, Maryland Avenue, Benning Road and Bladensburg Road Northeast. But they were overshadowed by the pair of military Humvees posted on one end of the plaza, with a half-dozen members of the National Guard standing alongside them.

They mostly kept watch, occasionally handing passers-by bottles of water, posing for pictures, and, at one point, yelling at a man to put down a rock as a potential argument seemed like it would escalate into a fight.

“This is the first time I’ve seen them sit right here,” said Omar Nash, a resident of the nearby Carver-Langston neighborhood who was on his way home from his job with the U.S. Postal Service. “I don’t understand why this is right here, why they have the trucks and stuff. That’s weird to me.”

But Nash also seemed both underwhelmed and unperturbed by the National Guard’s presence in the plaza, saying it made him feel neither threatened nor any safer.

“It doesn’t make a difference at all,” he said.

It’s been a year since President Donald Trump ordered the National Guard into D.C. as part of an effort to fight what he said were unacceptably high levels of crime. What started as a deployment of 800 troops — largely from the D.C. National Guard — has expanded as of early August to 4,630 troops, including from 15 states, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands.

The Guard’s presence has spurred loud protests and spawned ongoing litigation from the city’s attorney general to get them out, with many D.C. residents fretting that the National Guard is ill-equipped to police the city, and worrying that at worst Trump could more aggressively turn the troops against them.

Trump hasn’t only grown the National Guard’s numbers in D.C.; he has also expanded its deployment here until 2029. And as the Guard’s presence has grown, it has also become a new, if uncomfortable, norm for many residents — one made more frustrating by the city's lack of control over the decision.

“We don’t have no say in that shit,” said a frustrated resident in Anacostia, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly. “Even if the majority say no, it’s still going. Why is that possible?”

Groups of troops — many of them in their late teens and early 20s, roughly 60% of whom come from Republican-led Southern states — walking around the city’s neighborhoods are now a common sight; they’ve been spotted in Georgetown, Petworth, Trinidad, Capitol Hill and Columbia Heights, to name a few. They’re also showing up in parts of the city where hyperlocal problems have flared up: They deployed to Starburst Plaza after dozens of overdoses and posted up last week in LeDroit Park after a fatal shooting sparked fears of a retaliatory cycle of gun violence.
DSC00181 copy.jpg (6813x4542, AR: 1.50)At least 2,000 of the Guard members posted in D.C. will soon be immediate neighbors of many residents; the federal government said it would be spending $292 million to house the troops in apartments across the city over the next year.

“They’re nice overall,” said a man outside the Anacostia Metro station last week, where a pair of National Guard members stood nearby. “They’re helping in a certain way.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But civil rights advocates and some elected officials say that creeping normalization is precisely the danger.

“The idea that we are acclimating ourselves to armed National Guard members walking through our streets is perhaps the greatest risk of this deployment,” says Michael Perloff, an attorney for the ACLU of D.C. who is currently representing a D.C. resident and veteran who says she was assaulted and arrested by National Guard troops at her home in May.

“Because once you accept that the way you’re going to be policed is through armed military men,” he adds, “you’ve accepted a categorical escalation in the way that law enforcement is conducted.”

‘Extremely Expensive Photo Op’

The National Guard’s initial deployment in D.C. was nominally meant to assist the Metropolitan Police Department and federal law enforcement agencies to, as Trump said it, “rescue our nation’s capital from crime, bloodshed, bedlam, squalor, and worse” — even though D.C. officials countered that crime rates were decreasing quickly through Trump’s first year, before the deployment even happened.

"The spin has always been public safety, but anybody paying attention knows that crime was dropping before this," said Robert White, a D.C. Council member who is poised to become the District's next Congressional delegate.

During its first months, the Guard’s mission seemed disjointed. Troops patrolled commercial areas and tourist hubs like Union Station, leaving residents and local officials to sardonically marvel at how a crime-fighting mission avoided the city’s most violent neighborhoods. Within weeks, the mission inexplicably expanded to citywide maintenance tasks: cleaning parks, fixing benches and laying down mulch.
DC Federal Intervention (3471x2314, AR: 1.50)“Extremely expensive photo op, and you're paying for it,” tweeted D.C. police officer and former National Guard member Daniel Hodges.

While the removal of 500 tons of debris may have seemed to some a stretch of the National Guard’s mission, the U.S. Army said those tasks represented “visible proof of a unified commitment to restoring public trust, improving quality of life, and ensuring that the capital reflects the pride and dignity worthy of representing the American people.”

Over time, the mission also became more neighborhood-focused, with troops dispatched to areas experiencing overdoses or other public safety concerns, and even to help enforce teen curfew zones in late 2025 and earlier this year. Troops revived a mother who passed out in her car, helped a man who passed out in a Metro station and — as a NOTUS reporter watched — picked up litter at Starburst Plaza. Randy Clarke, general manager of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, said last week that the National Guard has been “more eyes and ears” in the system, helping make it safer for riders.
DSC01673 copy.jpg (6192x4128, AR: 1.50)Whether that outlay of troops and taxpayer dollars has accomplished the goal of helping lower crime in D.C. is a hotly contested topic. Trump certainly seems to think it has made the city safer. “Washington D.C. went from High Crime to NO CRIME,” he posted on Truth Social last month. Per MPD data, property crime has dropped 23% so far this year, compared to the same period last year. Violent crime is actually up 3%, though, largely driven by a significant spike in assaults with deadly weapons. At the same time, homicides are down 32%.

Independent researchers, however, say the federal surge appears to have accomplished something both measurable and narrow: an accelerated drop in opportunistic property crime, without a corresponding reduction in violent crime.

While crime was already declining before the troops arrived, a Niskanen Center analysis found that the broader federal emergency response coincided with a roughly 24% reduction in property crime during its first six months. Researchers cautioned they cannot isolate the Guard’s exact impact from the rest of the federal response, but noted the drop was most pronounced around transit hubs and commercial corridors where troops maintained a visible presence. Violent crime, however, remained unaffected.

“It does seem like low-level property crimes is something that really responds to manpower; if the guard goes away, we’ll lose that manpower,” said Richard Hahn, a senior manager for research and evidence at the Niskanen Center. But, he added, “it’s a really, really expensive way to keep low level property crimes under control — and by the way, these crimes are trending down anyway.”

‘Very Mixed Responses’

Brig. Gen. Leland Blanchard, the commander of the National Guard deployed in D.C., argues that his troops’ successes in the city are real and measurable.

Speaking during a news conference in early August, Blanchard said that over the past year the troops have provided 788 medical assists, reunited 43 lost children with their families, intervened in 262 altercations before they escalated further, and administered Narcan to 325 individuals. He added that the Guard also supported other law enforcement agencies 479 times over the year.

“The National Guard does not replace law enforcement,” Blanchard said. “We expand operational capacity, strengthen the ability to serve and provide additional capabilities during extraordinary circumstances.”

Blanchard said that the Guard’s presence at Starburst Plaza served that role; otherwise, MPD officers would have had to remain on site to ensure that no more overdoses happened. The Guard did the same last week in LeDroit Park, where it deployed two Humvees and eight Guard members.
National Guard in Washington (6819x4546, AR: 1.50)“There were very mixed responses,” Matt Fay, an advisory neighborhood commissioner in LeDroit Park, said of the Guard’s appearance in the neighborhood. “There were a number of people who said they appreciate it, but a number of people who said it made them nervous.”

Bethany Young, the deputy director of the D.C. Justice Lab, finds herself in the latter group, and said that while the presence of the Guard may discourage someone from stealing a car near a Metro station, it leaves the root causes of violence unaddressed.

“It’s dangerous to equate quiet, or things we can’t see, with safety,” Young says. “The decrease in opportunistic crime is not an indication that there has been a change in the preconditions that lead to crime.”

Brown Woodland, a violence interrupter in LeDroit Park, takes a nuanced view of having the Guard in D.C. posted in his neighborhood. “I guess it helps in the immediate area for a second,” he said. “But it’s just a patch until you uplift the people.”

A Billion-Dollar Extension

The deployment has also become one of Trump’s most expensive and enduring interventions in the District. The debate over its effectiveness cannot be separated from its staggering cost.

According to an analysis issued by the Congressional Budget Office this year, maintaining the troop posture cost $607 per Guard member daily, reaching over $330 million by early 2026. A more recent estimate submitted to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) said that maintaining the Guard’s presence in the city through the end of Trump’s term would cost an additional $1.4 billion. (That amount could cover MPD’s current budget for its 3,100 police officers for two years.)

Janeese Lewis George, the Ward 4 council member and Democratic nominee for D.C. mayor, calls the deployment “nothing more than astronomically expensive political theater” and an “anti-democratic boondoggle that hurts tourism and normalizes the militarization of our cities.”

Jason Ziedenberg, research director at the D.C. Justice Lab, offers another way to measure that spending: He estimates the cost of just a few days of the deployment could fully fund trauma recovery centers for crime survivors in all eight wards of the District. While federal Guard funding could not be simply redirected into the city’s coffers, advocates say the contrast highlights a federal willingness to fund rapid enforcement over long-term community investments.
Pete Hegseth (7374x4916, AR: 1.50)“Sinking scarce dollars into a failed operation is happening at a time when Americans across the country, but particularly D.C. residents, are facing an affordability crisis,” said Tazra Mitchell, chief policy officer at the D.C. Fiscal Policy Institute.

The deployment’s costs extend beyond the federal price tag. While the National Guard itself does not make arrests, the troops serve as the highly visible manifestation of a broader federal response. Their deployment coincided with aggressive shifts in policing, prosecution and detention that placed growing pressure on the District’s criminal justice system, driving the local jail population up 18% over the past year.

According to D.C. Courts data, criminal filings have nearly tripled since fiscal 2023 — surging from about 7,000 cases to more than 18,000 — even as the court system operated through four years of essentially flat funding. As a result, the courts’ criminal case clearance rate has fallen from 108% in fiscal 2023 to 60% in fiscal 2025.

Misty Thomas Zaleski, executive director of the Council for Court Excellence, cautioned against blaming the Guard itself for the gridlock, pointing instead to the lack of legal infrastructure.

“Public safety doesn’t stop with an arrest,” Zaleski said. “It is more expensive to incarcerate a person than it is to provide them housing, social safety-net services and health care.”

‘Remind People That It’s Not Normal’

A year on, Young of the D.C. Justice Lab says community groups have seen a profound chilling effect driven by a critical oversight gap: Unlike local police, federal troops fall entirely outside the District’s Office of Police Complaints. That lack of local accountability, combined with a fear of federal entanglement, has had tangible human consequences, she said.

Some schools have had to arrange alternative student transportation because parents are too afraid to walk their children past armed patrols, while trauma service providers report that crime victims are skipping healing services to avoid encounters with federal personnel.

Advocates say the questions of accountability and public trust will likely outlast the deployment itself.
DC Federal Intervention (8078x5386, AR: 1.50)“Safety for most people cannot be quantified or measured by the number of armed people in uniform that you see walking around the community,” Young added. 

Many D.C. residents and elected officials remain steadfast in their opposition to having the National Guard deployed across the city — and they express it in ways big and small. Convincing Trump to reverse course is unlikely, so Free D.C., the advocacy organization leading protests against the deployment, has launched a postcard-writing campaign to governors providing troops to build political pressure to pull them out.

Gail Sullivan, a Free D.C. adviser and longtime resident of the east end of Capitol Hill, says she regularly uses her neighborhood’s WhatsApp group (somewhat jokingly called the “People’s Front of H Street”) to warn neighbors when troops are walking around. She, though, chooses to directly engage with them.
DC0A6777 copy.jpg (7345x4897, AR: 1.50)“Most of the time I’m saying, ‘Who’s looking after your family?’ But now I’m going to change it. I’m going to say, ‘How would you like it that every time your family came out of their house there was an armed National Guardsman walking around?’ That’s a way to look at it from a personal point of view,” she said.

Karen Degraphenreid, an organizer with Free D.C. who also served in the U.S. Air Force for 10 years before leaving earlier this year, says she has found herself conflicted with how she feels about the people who are serving in the National Guard and what they are being told to do in D.C.

“They are not these horrible baby killers, but they are enabling something that is dangerous,” she says. “They aren’t doing the ICE arrests, but if ICE told them to create a perimeter, they would. So at the end of the day, my feelings about how nice they are as people don’t matter as much as, ‘Hey, you’re enabling this occupation.’”

Looking ahead after a year of having the National Guard in D.C., Degraphenreid says she keeps focused on a single message: “We have these conversations to remind people that it’s not normal,” she says. “We’re shouting from the rooftops trying to make sure people don’t get too comfortable.”

entries.title: What $800,000 Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (With Solar Panels)
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the DMV.
entries.content:
Soak up the sun, Sheryl Crow says. But it’s harder for homes to lighten up their electric bills now that most federal solar power tax credits have expired. (Prior to 2026, the IRS covered 30% of installation costs for eligible homeowners.) This week, we set out to find homes in the DMV that already have solar panels installed and can yield major utility savings without massive upfront costs.

Real estate professionals we spoke with cautioned that it's important to do extra legwork when shopping for homes with solar panels. Ask to see utility bill data. Make sure the roof wasn’t damaged in the installation process. And think through whether you’ll use enough daytime electricity to take advantage of solar panels; a family of four able to do laundry by day will better harness the sun than two people who work 9-to-5 jobs in office buildings.

We did notice that lower price-point solar panel homes are much more plentiful in the District than in the burbs. With that in mind, take a look at this trio of eco-friendly options.

Have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.

D.C.

Untitled
The listing: 318 Varnum St. NW

The price: $850,000

The specifics: A century-old rowhouse with 21st-century solar power. We found this three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in a quiet corner of Petworth, a few blocks from President Abraham Lincoln’s cottage and acres of walking trails at Rock Creek Cemetery. The house is carefully remodeled, with a contemporary kitchen, hardwood floors and potential guest quarters (with a second kitchen) in the basement.

The solar panels: This home has a new roof and south-facing solar panels, for maximum energy production without worrisome leaks. There’s also an e-bike charging station.

Sell us on it: “Tucked away on a quiet, tree-lined street, you’re only a quick stroll from local parks and the Metro,” Compass listing agent Ryan DaSilva writes. “It’s efficient, it’s stylish, and it’s ready for you to add your personal touch.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Maryland

Untitled
The listing: 17613 Kirk Lane, Rockville

The price: $759,000

The specifics: An eco-friendly family dreamhouse, this Rockville Cape Cod has solar panels, a vehicle-charging station and a greenhouse. The current owners loved raising kids in this suburban home on a 1-acre lot, with four bedrooms, three bathrooms and a finished basement. The house is 3 miles from suburban amenities in Olney and even closer to several parks, a meditation center and the Norbeck Hills Pool.

The solar panels: The current owner’s utility bill was less than $100 in seven months out of 12. The only spike was a $516 bill in January 2026, according to data shared with NOTUS. (In Montgomery County, real estate agents are required to share utility records with prospective owners.) In September 2025, the home produced more electricity than it used, resulting in a $21 credit.

Sell us on it: “This home is ideal for an owner seeking energy efficiency but who may not like the look of panels,” said Tony Krichbaum, a real estate agent with The Rollings Team in Olney. He said the panels are on the rear roof and face southeast for maximum sun exposure. “Bonus for purchasers who have an electric vehicle or are looking for one: The charging station adds nothing to utility bills and is an incredibly rare feature.”

Virginia

Untitled
The listing: 1306 Commonwealth Ave., Alexandria

The price: $825,000

The specifics: This solar-paneled Del Ray home was such a catch, it sold after Compass broker Kerry Adams shared photos and utility data with NOTUS. The three-bedroom, three-bathroom, 1,750-square-foot townhome also had the highest price per square foot of any listing with solar panels that we found in the DMV. But homes in Del Ray fetch top dollar, and this one is only a 10-minute walk from the Braddock Road Metro station.

The solar panels: Since January 2025, the electric bill for this home hit triple digits only four times. But overall, the Dominion Energy bill averages a negligible $8.70.

Sell us on it: “"One of the biggest challenges for buyers looking for a home in Del Ray is the cost of ownership,” Adams said. “That's where this home stands apart. Energy-efficient solar panels keep most monthly Dominion Energy bills under $10, helping offset the cost of living.”

entries.title: Ex-Biden Officials Are Planning How to Build Back the Government Post-DOGE
entries.summary: Their proposals range from a new agency to overhauling federal workers’ pay.
entries.content:
Former Biden administration officials are contending with a new reality: Future administrations won’t have a choice but to confront the way the Trump administration has disrupted how the government works.

That’s the premise of a new set of proposals published Tuesday in the law and policy journal Just Security, authored by several former Biden officials and experts at think tanks.

“We have a lot of rebuilding to do,” K. Sabeel Rahman, one of the authors of the plan, told NOTUS. “Our ambition shouldn’t be just limited to gluing the broken pieces of the vase back together.”

Rahman, a law professor at Cornell Law School, previously worked for the Biden administration as the acting head of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.

The papers propose a complete reorientation of the government so that it’s more responsive to presidential orders, emergencies and everyday work. To do this, the authors are calling for a new Cabinet-level agency that brings together all federal administrative work under one roof, from HR to technology to financial management.

Other ideas include overhauling the pay structure for federal employees to better compete with the private sector and a campaign to rewrite the federal workforce’s collective bargaining rights.

The new project, dubbed the “Reinvention Blueprints,” is technically viewpoint neutral, platforming ideas from experts. Its authors say their intended audience is the next “rule of law administration,” said Dani Schulkin, director of democracy initiatives at Just Security who previously worked on national security issues for the Biden administration. 

Abuses of power can seem like more obvious threats, but the proposals to enable the government to do things like deliver safety-net benefits or protect people from exploitative consumer products are just as important, Rahman said, noting that “democracy can fail in many ways.”

Tara Dawson McGuinness and Amira Boland, from the liberal think tank New America, are behind the proposal for a new agency — a "Department of Services” — to be charged with making the government work.

They’re also pitching the establishment of “delivery units” in federal agencies and, within the White House, a deputy chief of staff for implementation charged with making sure the government is delivering. They’d have a “National Delivery Unit” in the White House to help solve complex problems across multiple agencies.

Loren DeJonge Schulman and Rob Shriver — both former Biden appointees now working at Federation of American Scientists and Democracy Forward, respectively — published a paper Tuesday on the civil service, arguing that it’s not set up to deliver, either. They want Congress to reset collective bargaining rights for government workers, modernize government hiring and more.

The focus on delivery isn’t totally new. Then-President Barack Obama, for example, created the White House tech team that Trump remade into DOGE last year. That initiative was developed in 2014 in the wake of the high-profile HealthCare.gov crash, a failure that threatened the success of one of Obama’s signature policies.

But McGuinness and Boland say their proposal is meant to fundamentally reorient the government instead of offering an ad hoc solution.

“This is a roadmap for people who want the government to work,” McGuinness said.

McGuinness also helped author a child-care proposal for “Project 2029,” another playbook of policy proposals for future Democratic presidential candidates.

Democrats have become laser-focused on good governance in the aftermath of Trump’s DOGE initiative — a campaign that proved to be deeply controversial with the American public.

Chad Maisel, the executive director of Project 2029, told NOTUS that making sure its proposals are actually implementable is a core priority. Focusing on the “nuts and bolts of government” hasn’t always been a priority for Democratic presidential candidates, but now, “the idea of a government that works … is so core to the political discourse.”

entries.title: The New Normal
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: One year of the National Guard in D.C., a serious strain on city courts and the latest from Commanders training camp.





THE LATEST

It was a year ago today that President Donald Trump declared he was deploying the National Guard and hundreds of federal law enforcement agents to combat what he said were unacceptably high levels of crime in D.C.

The initial deployment of troops was small: roughly 800 of them, mostly from the D.C. National Guard. But that number has grown dramatically, with some 4,600 troops from more than a dozen states — most led by Republican governors — now patrolling the city. For context, consider that D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department has just over 3,100 officers.

The deployment initially drew angry protests, and many D.C. residents told NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle and Michael Brice-Saddler that they are still mad about what they derisively call an occupation. Other people credit the National Guard for the decrease in overall crime that the city has experienced, while the reality is mixed: Researchers say that the troops have helped drive down some property crimes, but that violent crime takes more work than just posting a Humvee with a few troops on a street corner.

“I guess it helps in the immediate area for a second,” a violence interrupter in LeDroit Park, where the Guard recently posted up in response to concerns of shootings, told NOTUS. “But it’s just a patch until you uplift the people.”

No matter where you stand on the National Guard in D.C., one thing is clear: It’s expensive. While it's hard to determine the overall cost of the deployment, the Congressional Budget Office estimated this year that the first five months cost more than $300 million — roughly $607 per guardsman per day. The Pentagon recently told Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) that keeping the Guard in D.C. through January 2029 would cost an estimated $1.4 billion more.

Despite simmering frustration with the deployment, plenty of D.C. residents seem resigned to the new normal. Not only are troops expected to stay around until 2029, but some 2,000 of them will be moving into apartments across the city (at a cost of almost $300 million through next year). But that normalization is exactly what some activists and elected officials are so concerned about.

“Once you accept that the way you’re going to be policed is through armed military men,” said Michael Perloff of the ACLU of D.C., “you’ve accepted a categorical escalation in the way that law enforcement is conducted.”

National Guard Union Station (6192x4128, AR: 1.50)



DEEP DIVE

D.C. courts are warning they’ve hit a breaking point. While the deployment of the Guard and the federal law enforcement surge are adding pressure to local court operations, officials say the judicial system has been operating with essentially flat funding for four years — leaving them pleading for a financial lifeline to keep cases moving.

In a Washington Post op-ed, D.C. Court of Appeals Chief Judge Anna Blackburne-Rigsby and Superior Court Chief Judge Milton Lee Jr. declared that the courts “lack the operational capacity needed to administer justice.”

Rather than increase funding, House appropriators who set the courts’ budget are proposing a  6% cut, even as criminal cases have nearly tripled since fiscal year 2023 — rising from 6,993 to 18,214 cases.

That strain has coincided with the criminal case clearance rate — or the number of cases completed compared to the number of new cases filed — falling from 108% in 2023 to 60% in 2025 as incoming cases outpace capacity.

While the Senate confirmed eight new local judges last week to help ease the city’s longstanding vacancy crisis, court leaders warn that extra judges alone won’t solve the problem. Court spokesman Doug Buchanan noted in a statement that adding judges without funding essential courtroom staff, security officers and IT infrastructure leaves D.C. courts hamstrung amid the federal government’s broader enforcement surge.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Some D.C. bus drivers aren’t adhering to a WMATA directive that they quote the fare, saying it could cause confrontations, The Washington Post reports. Bus drivers in surrounding communities that have gone fare-free, such as Alexandria, have said that they no longer fear retaliation.

The Trump administration will ask the Supreme Court to reverse a federal judge’s ruling that stopped the $400 million White House ballroom project, the president said last week. A federal appeals court recently upheld U.S. District Judge Richard Leon’s ruling from this spring that Trump would need congressional approval before constructing a massive ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

Whine country: City Cast DC broke down what locals complained about to 311 in July, which most often was (surprise surprise) trash and parking enforcement.

The Federal Aviation Administration announced it will temporarily suspend flight operations at National Airport on Aug. 23 because of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, Fox5 reports.





WHAT YOU GET WITH SOLAR PANELS


Rockville real estate (1440x961, AR: 1.50)
Listed for $759,000, this Cape Cod has four bedrooms, three bathrooms, solar panels, a vehicle-charging station and a greenhouse.

Click to guess where this listing is sold:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia 
  3. D.C.
We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.





SPORTS

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that it was not a happy Monday in Ashburn as the Commanders confirmed starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps over the weekend. For now, the five-time Pro Bowler will be replaced by third-year lineman Brandon Coleman, who was the starting left tackle as a rookie in 2024 and served as a backup last fall.

"You never know what happens," Coleman said after practice. "You always want to be ready."

entries.title: Survey Says …
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Polling vs. Democratic primary voters, again. Trump’s secret AF1 swap. Data center builders like Ken Paxton. Chuck Edwards’ replacement. Food industry vs. RFK Jr. Plus: Social Security reform lives, sorta. 





THE LATEST

Is tonight another major test for pollsters? Public polling fell flat on its face in last week’s Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, where widespread predictions of a landslide for Abdul El-Sayed proved completely off the mark. El-Sayed won, but in a squeaker that allowed anyone’s narrative to be real. The result has led many supporters of David Crowley, the mainline Democratic candidate in tonight’s Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, to scoff at polls finding progressive Francesca Hong with an all-but-insurmountable lead.

“This is not going to be the runaway that some of the polls suggest that it will be,” Sachin Chheda, a Democratic consultant in Wisconsin who has stayed neutral in the race, told NOTUS’ Christa Dutton.

Maybe pollsters just can’t poll Democratic primaries anymore? That’s a theory gaining steam after Michigan. The polling certainly is a real mess in Wisconsin, mostly because the race itself is a real mess. The latest available poll, an internal one released by Crowley’s campaign, shows Hong up 19. The Crowley campaign called that good news. They get to call it whatever they want, because it is the only poll of the field as it actually stands available to public eyes. All previous polling had one or both of the two candidates who dropped out — Sara Rodriguez and Mandela Barnes — included. (Oh, also like 265,000 voters cast early ballots already, many before those two dropped.)

Charles Franklin, guru of polling at Marquette University Law School, says it’s important to note that every public poll has found Hong up big. When one pollster made an attempt to adjust its findings to the shifting landscape, she was still in the lead.

“As a pollster, you don’t want to say to people, ‘Everything I’m telling you is complete garbage’ — I don’t believe that. But, ‘What I’m telling you is hopefully informative,’” he said. “But anybody would be foolish to bet the house literally on a poll result.”

OK fine, Wisconsin can’t prove primary polls still work. What about Minnesota? The latest public polling of the pitched battle between centrist Rep. Angie Craig and progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the Democratic Senate primary has found either Flanagan up by a lot, or the race to be a dead heat. Go fish!

Open tabs: Contiguous US breaks its record for hottest month ever (AP); Judge Temporarily Blocks Mamdani’s Pied-à-Terre Tax (WSJ); Taylor Swift songs removed from White House, Trump campaign posts (Reuters); A.I.-Driven Chip Crunch Leads to New Rush of Lobbying in Washington (NYT)





From the White House


WaPo’s Air Force One scoop reopens the case of the NATO trip: A blockbuster story from The Washington Post last night details how Donald Trump was snuck out of the presidential aircraft via a catering truck while leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month. The Post reports Trump was then taken to another Air Force VIP plane (one of the smaller ones traditionally associated with VP travel) and flown out of Turkey while the press was told he was departing with them on the original 747. The change was reportedly prompted by fears of an attempt on Trump’s life by Iran. You’ll recall this was the trip when Trump had to send his new Qatari-donated plane away without him on it, reportedly in response to security concerns. Trump has since said the Qatari plane is being upgraded.

The New York Times confirmed much of the Post’s reporting last night, noting the unscheduled presidential movements suggest the Iranian threat was taken quite seriously by officials.

From the campaign trail


Are data center builders making their Senate pick in Texas? Republican nominee Ken Paxton has called the data center issue “complicated” and mostly avoided the subject. Democratic nominee James Talarico has laid out specific plans for tighter regulations around data center construction. NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno reports that the industry is siding with Paxton — his federal campaign arms have received at least $448,000 from executives and political committees of companies building or operating data centers.

Rep. Chuck Edwards’ ballot replacement: State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom is the new Republican nominee in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District after the incumbent Edwards withdrew from the race, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports. The district’s GOP executive committee selected her from a slate of five candidates. Balkcorn has been in the state General Assembly since 2023, and will face Democratic nominee Jamie Ager in November.





THE BIG ONE

The lame-duck session will be all about Social Security if a bipartisan group of senators intent on reforming the program has its way. NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports on a plan led by led by retiring Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) to take advantage of the stretch between the November election and the seating of the new Congress in January to jump on one of American politics’ most dangerous third rails: Social Security reform.

The plan: Pass a bill that tasks an independent, bipartisan board with figuring out how to keep the program solvent for the next 50 years, likely by doing things people don’t love, Jeff writes. The bill would also create special rules to streamline its path to the Senate floor. In theory, the upcoming departure of about a dozen senators this fall means those lawmakers can vote for the bill free of political consequence.

The opposition is vocal and powerful. AARP is rallying its millions of members to oppose it. Americans for Tax Reform’s Grover Norquist is trying to stop it, too, calling it an effort to force Republicans to support tax hikes.

The state of things: The Senate Finance Committee held a hearing on the bill last week, a first step toward real advancement. But, a Senate Democratic aide told Jeff, “I will eat my shoe” if the bill passes.

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: After a Year in D.C., the National Guard Seems Almost Normal, by Martin and Michael Brice-Saddler

What $800,000 Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia Real Estate (With Solar Panels), by Rebecca Ritzel





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Baseball’s trade deadline showed, yet again, how extreme wealth and inequality undermine basic fairness — or at least the perception of fairness — in the sport, writes Matt K. Lewis today at NOTUS Perspectives. Kind of like in the American economy as a whole. No wonder socialism is in vogue.





NEW ON NOTUS

The food industry sighs relief at new “ultra-processed” rules: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. proposed new rules around the so-called “generally recognized as safe” regulatory loophole that were nowhere near as bad as industry feared they might be, NOTUS’ Paige Winfield Cunningham reports. Under the proposed guidelines, food manufacturers would have to submit information about additives, including dyes, preservatives, sweeteners and emulsifiers, to the FDA — but the “ultra-processed foods” RFK Jr. has railed about for years would remain on store shelves.

What’s more, the proposal would require congressional action before getting any real teeth, which gives industry more opportunity to flex its considerable lobbying muscle.

entries.title: A Group of Centrist Senators Sees a Window to Overhaul Social Security
entries.summary: AARP is already lobbying against the bipartisan effort.
entries.content:
A group of eight centrist senators is attempting to compel Congress to revamp Social Security, in what many in Washington see as the first real effort at overhauling the government's biggest program in more than a decade.

The push, led by retiring Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), sets the stage for a major confrontation later this year with potential consequences for the 59 million seniors who currently receive benefits.

Their bill, the PROMISE Act, does not directly cut Social Security benefits or raise taxes to avert the program’s approaching budget shortfall. Rather, it would task a bipartisan board with writing a plan to keep the pension system funded for another 50 years, likely through trillions of dollars in tax hikes and benefit cuts. The legislation would also establish parliamentary rules aimed at pushing Congress to act on the board’s proposal.

Even if it passes, the bill would likely only spawn another fight over Social Security in the next Congress, which would still have to approve the board’s proposal to be pushed into law. But senior groups are mobilizing now to stop what they see as an effort to slash retiree benefits, while deficit hawks argue failure to act risks putting the U.S. government on a dangerously unsustainable debt trajectory.

The group of eight is targeting the “lame duck” period after the November midterm elections but before the new Congress begins in January as their best chance of success. President Donald Trump has promised to reject cuts to Social Security, and former President Joe Biden never pursued a deal with Republicans on the program.

“This is the first time that Social Security solvency has gotten serious legislative attention on a bipartisan basis in several decades,” said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a centrist think-tank that supports the plan. “It is a major breakthrough in conversations that have long been stagnant.”

As it stands, Congress has roughly six years to pass legislation before automatic reductions as large as 25% snap into effect for Social Security beneficiaries, according to the latest estimates by the Social Security Board of Trustees. The wave of baby boomers exiting the workforce and entering retirement, coupled with generally longer lifespans, has meant that the program’s payment costs exceed its incoming tax revenues.

There has been no consensus about how to head off this long-approaching cliff. In December 2010, a bipartisan commission led by Republican Alan Simpson and Democrat Erskine Bowles proposed roughly $4 trillion in deficit reduction measures in benefits cuts and tax hikes. President Barack Obama and Republican House Speaker John Boehner came close to a deal on the “Simpson-Bowles” proposal, but it fell apart and similar talks have never since resumed.

The current plan grew out of Durbin's conversations with Bowles, to whom the senator vented in private conversations that Congress was not dealing with big issues like Social Security, according to a Durbin aide.

Durbin began meeting last year with colleagues about legislation to force floor action on Social Security, and Durbin held a meeting in his office in early September 2025 with Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), Angus King (I-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), Cassidy and Senate Finance Chair Mike Crapo (R-Idaho). Durbin and Crapo were the last two members of the Senate to have served on Simpson-Bowles.

The PROMISE Act that emerged tasks the existing Social Security Advisory Board with coming up with a plan to extend the program’s solvency for 50 years, starting from the point of passage. That board has seven seats, only four of which are currently filled — two by Democrats and two by Republicans.

The bill would then be referred to the Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee. If those committees do not advance the measure, the bill would be automatically discharged to the floor of each chamber. To be incorporated into the bill, any amendments would also have to extend Social Security’s solvency for a half-century.

Last Wednesday, the Senate Finance Committee held its first hearing about the PROMISE Act, the first step toward a vote.

Even without including concrete policy changes, this proposal faces significant hurdles.

Trump would have to face charges that he’s abandoning a core campaign pledge since the 2016 presidential election. (A White House spokesperson declined to comment.)

AARP — the roughly 40-million-members-strong seniors’ organization — has begun urging lawmakers to reject the bill, highlighting polling that suggests 85% of Americans support maintaining or increasing benefits. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) has begun calling for Senate Democrats to reject benefit cuts and instead stand behind financing Social Security by repealing the existing limit on payroll taxes for those earning more than $184,500 per year, arguing “the Democratic Party is ever to regain the faith of ordinary Americans it must stand firm on the issue of Social Security.”

Even conservatives who have long called for Social Security reform are mobilizing against it. Grover Norquist, the antitax crusader who leads the conservative Americans for Tax Reform, said in an interview that he has begun lobbying congressional Republican leadership to oppose the bill. Norquist called the legislation a "very real effort by the left" to convince Republicans to support tax hikes.

One Senate Democratic aide, granted anonymity to candidly assess legislative dynamics, said, “I will eat my shoe” if the bill passes this year.

Durbin acknowledged those odds: “Miracles do occur,” he said.

In another potential sign of the legislation’s radioactivity, half of its original sponsors — Cassidy, Durbin, Tillis and Republican John Cornyn of Texas — are leaving the Senate at the end of this year. (Cassidy and Cornyn lost their primaries against Trump-backed challengers.)

A fifth, King, is 82 and will not face voters again until 2030, should he choose to run again.

But supporters are adamant that Washington is running out of time to act, particularly given recent tremors in the economy. The federal debt has exacerbated volatility in the bond market and raised borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and more. It is possible to fund the Social Security trust shortfall by issuing more debt, but that could drive interest rates only further.

“The bond market could force senators to come to the table,” said Ben Harris, vice president and director of Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank. Harris was skeptical the legislation would pass, but added: “Trump has pledged to leave Social Security benefits untouched, but Trump has also done a lot of things he promised he’d never do. I think there is potentially a window.”

The legislation’s backers also say the proposal, by making an independent board responsible for crafting the policy, is carefully designed to insulate lawmakers from political pressure.

“Groups on the left and right will demagogue it, and it’s an uphill battle,” said Marc Goldwein, senior vice president for the nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. “But it’s pretty low risk because you’re asking the Social Security Advisory Board, basically a bunch of nonpoliticians, to come up with a plan.”

The attempt to shield lawmakers from the bill’s political ramifications is part of what most frustrates its opponents. The upcoming departure of about a dozen senators this fall means those lawmakers can vote for the bill free of political consequence. Trump is not going to face voters again.

Durbin's office denies that the legislation amounts to a "fast track" or a "commission" bill, pointing out that it preserves the typical Senate procedure by requiring 60 votes for passage.

That’s not how Social Security advocates see it. Alex Lawson, executive director of Social Security Works, a progressive group founded during the Obama administration to oppose cuts to the program, summed up the legislation as creating “a process with less input from the public to cut Social Security in the least democratic way possible.”

“But you do have to worry, and we are worried,” he said. “They always try in the least accountable moment. For all the times they have failed, they only have to succeed one time for seniors to lose.”

entries.title: An Ohio Congressman Violated the STOCK Act With 22 Late Disclosures
entries.summary: Rep. Michael Rulli failed to properly reveal trades in Palantir, Pfizer and several tech giants.
entries.content:
Rep. Michael Rulli failed to properly disclose 22 personal stock trades, according to a NOTUS review of new congressional financial records, making him the latest member of Congress to violate a federal insider trading and transparency law.

The Ohio Republican was months late revealing that he had bought or sold shares in companies including defense and immigration contractor Palantir, pharmaceutical giant Pfizer and several tech companies, such as Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle.

Rulli is a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over telecommunications, consumer protection, drug safety, energy policy, and interstate and foreign commerce.

Together, Rulli’s tardy trades are worth between $22,022 and $330,000 — lawmakers are only required to disclose their trades in broad ranges — and the oldest are from late 2024, congressional financial records indicate.

The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act requires members of Congress to publicly disclose individual stock trades no later than 45 days after making them.

Rulli’s congressional office acknowledged NOTUS’ request for comment Monday but did not otherwise respond to questions, including whether he paid a fine for his late disclosures. House Ethics Committee-administered penalties begin at $200.

A freshman lawmaker, Rulli is one of the wealthiest members of Ohio’s congressional delegation, according to NOTUS’ Capitol Gains project, which tracks wealth of federal lawmakers.

Rulli’s STOCK Act disclosure violation coincides with a Republican-backed effort in Congress to ban federal lawmakers from buying individual stocks at all. The Stop Insider Trading Act passed the House in July and awaits consideration in the Senate. Rulli voted in favor of the bill.Dozens of federal lawmakers have failed to comply with the existing STOCK Act, which Congress passed in 2012 to govern its own members’ behavior regarding the intersection of their personal finances and duties to the public.

Just this week, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), who supports a ban on members of Congress trading stock, violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure rules by failing to properly disclose a six-figure stock share exchange from 2025 and made by his wife.

Wyden spokesperson Hank Stern told Politico, which first reported the violation, that the transaction “was discovered when filing the annual report and not subject to penalty from the ethics committee” and that “the senator’s wife is an independent small businesswoman whose finances are separate from her husband.” Wyden’s Senate office acknowledged NOTUS’ request for comment Monday but did not otherwise respond to phone and email messages.

Other senators who’ve violated the STOCK Act during the past year include Sens. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

In the House, STOCK Act violators include Reps. Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

entries.title: Florida AG Wields State Pension Fund Against the NYT
entries.summary: James Uthmeier is claiming that the Florida retirement fund’s investment in the Times allows it to request internal documents and push for editorial changes.
entries.content:
Florida’s Republican attorney general is employing a novel strategy in an attempt to prove “editorial malpractice” at The New York Times — seeking to use his control over the state’s pension fund, which invests in the media company, to compel the release of private documents that he claims will prove the company faces substantial harm due to bias.

James Uthmeier, Florida’s top law enforcement officer, sent a 28-page letter to the Times on Monday requesting internal documents related to the newspaper’s board of directors.

Uthmeier gave the board two weeks to respond, and threatened to file suit if it does not answer.

This is at least the third letter the Times has received this year regarding potential lawsuits from shareholders demanding it turn over records related to its coverage, but the first from a sitting government official.

Uthmeier lists four instances where he says the media company used an “interested or unnamed source” to publish a claim without independent verification, and later had to issue a correction.

They include the scandal around a 2020 podcast called “Caliphate,” where the central source was found to have lied and was later charged by Canadian authorities. The Times launched an internal investigation and called the incident an "institutional failing.”

Uthmeier also cited a correction the newspaper issued regarding the cause of death of a U.S. Capitol Police officer during the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot; an editor's note issued on a story that said it “relied too heavily on claims made by Hamas”; and an opinion piece by Nicholas Kristof on the alleged rape of Palestinian prisoners in Israel.

Danielle Rhoades Ha, a spokesperson for The New York Times, told NOTUS in a statement that the letter “is a clear attempt to chill First Amendment-protected journalism.”

As part of his role as Florida’s attorney general, Uthmeier serves as legal counsel for the State Board of Administration, which manages the state’s public pension funds. Those accounts own a collective 160,000 shares of NYT stock.

Uthmeier is seeking to use that influence to demand six years of internal board documents. He says that although the First Amendment protects speech, the company cannot ignore the demands of its shareholders.

In his letter, Uthmeier states that his investigation is “grounded in concrete corporate risk,” as opposed to “general dissatisfaction with editorial judgement.” He alleges that there are documented instances of the media company inadequately applying editorial standards to stories in its opinion section, and that his duty to oversee Florida’s public-sector pension program gives him the right to investigate.

Uthmeier takes particular issue with a piece that ran in the Times’ opinion section, headlined “The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians,” which claimed in part that Israeli soldiers had committed assaults against Palestinian prisoners — including the use of dogs to commit rape. The piece prompted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to threaten a lawsuit that has not yet been filed.

In his demand letter, Uthmeier asks for records detailing conversations with the board of directors regarding that opinion piece, as well as others. In his letter, he said that he was not asking the Times’ to “change news coverage or retract an article,” instead claiming that he was simply overseeing a risky investment.

“What matters here is that a host of red flags, presumably shown to the Board, establish that the Company suffers from biased reporting practices that threaten, in the Board’s own words, the Company’s ‘key assets’: its ‘brand’ and ‘reputation,’” Uthmeier wrote.

entries.title: DOJ Wants Executive Privilege to Cover Trump’s Private Advisers
entries.summary: The protections have historically applied only to the president and his top staff.
entries.content:
A Justice Department memo published this week says President Donald Trump’s private advisers may claim executive privilege when asked to hand over their communications, a move that would greatly expand the historical protections upheld by the Supreme Court in multiple rulings.

Executive privilege is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, but the high court has held that the U.S. government’s separation of powers permits the president to keep certain correspondence confidential — making it more difficult for Congress and the courts to subpoena certain information.

“Executive privilege can apply to presidential communications with private advisers so long as the communications relate to official presidential decisionmaking, involve or reflect communications with the President or his direct advisers, and are confidential,” Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser wrote in a memo opinion published Monday.

The memo broadly defines who qualifies as a private adviser to include anyone outside of the executive branch, “whether they be members of the public, state officials, or employees of other branches of the federal government.”

The Supreme Court defined the protection in United States v. Nixon, when President Richard Nixon tried to claim the shield over secret tapes in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal. The justices ruled in 1974 that executive privilege is not absolute and does not apply in criminal cases, and the protection has historically applied only to the president and immediate White House advisers.

This is the first time the Justice Department has explicitly expanded the protection to individuals outside the White House, including private citizens. The policy is likely to prompt a legal challenge, and it remains unclear whether the courts will allow the expansion of the decades-old definition of the protection.

Trump has attempted to exert executive privilege several times since his first term in office to shield himself from congressional scrutiny and court proceedings.

In 2019, the president attempted to use the protections while seeking to stop publication of Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s full, unredacted report into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election.

Trump has also made several attempts to use executive privilege to block the release of information related to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Last month, a D.C. federal appeals court unanimously upheld the criminal conviction of Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s top trade advisers, after he refused to testify in front of Congress and provide documents in connection to a Jan. 6 probe. Navarro had attempted to appeal his conviction by citing the protections of executive privilege.

When the FBI searched Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in 2022 to seize classified documents Trump possessed while he was not a sitting president, Trump also attempted to exert executive privilege protection.

entries.title: Federal Employees Can Use TikTok Again
entries.summary: The reversal comes weeks after the Trump administration launched TikTok accounts following updated DOJ guidance on the social media app.
entries.content:
The White House reversed a ban prohibiting TikTok on government devices this week — allowing federal government employees to start using the popular social media platform again.

The memo overturns a ban prohibiting use of the app on federal devices signed into law by then-President Joe Biden in 2022. The Office of Management and Budget was tasked with creating guidelines for enforcing the ban, with exceptions for “law enforcement activities” and “national security interests.”

“TikTok is no longer a ‘covered application’ for purposes of the No TikTok on Government Devices Act,” OMB Director Russell Vought wrote in the short memo.

TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the policy reversal.

The app’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, sold a majority of its shares to U.S. investors in January after facing pressure from the federal government over national security concerns. The Justice Department issued new guidance on the policy last month, saying the restructuring allows the U.S. version — backed by stakeholders like Oracle — to once again be downloaded on federal devices.

Several agencies launched new accounts on July 21 following the DOJ’s guidance, including cinematic videos and compilations featuring Trump and Cabinet leaders.

The White House launched its own TikTok account last August — a year before the ban was rescinded.

Lawmakers had been pushing to ban TikTok for all American users for years, and a 2024 law required ByteDance to divest in its U.S. operations or face a nationwide ban. Some members of Congress took issue with the White House’s use of the platform at the time due to national security concerns.

entries.title: Trump Backs FIFA President Amid Resignation Pressure
entries.summary: Gianni Infantino lost the confidence of global soccer organizations when he suggested third-party investments in World Cup commercialization.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump has stepped in to defend FIFA President Gianni Infantino, throwing his weight behind a staunch ally as calls for the international soccer boss’ resignation have reached a fever pitch.

Trump had earlier distanced himself from the FIFA president’s proposal to sell off private stakes in the World Cup, which resulted in an escalating conflict from which Infantino was forced to backtrack.

“FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino,” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social. “If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!”

Trump’s comments come in direct contrast to the position CONCACAF, the federation in charge of U.S. soccer, took in response to Infantino’s privatization scheme.

Infantino was forced to drop the idea earlier this month, acknowledging the project had created “divisions of a nature that … are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.”

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” CONCACAF wrote in an “open letter to the football family” on Monday, joined by Asia and Europe’s confederations. The organization has repeatedly suggested it has both lost confidence in Infantino’s leadership and is seeking avenues for accountability, including the FIFA president’s resignation.

Infantino is in hot water with the U.S. for other reasons, too: Weeks after this year’s World Cup ended, host cities are still chasing FIFA for millions of dollars they believe the governing body had promised them, The Athletic reported.

Infantino had developed a close relationship with Trump leading up to this year’s World Cup, which was jointly hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico. Infantino also reportedly ran his privatization proposal by figures within Trump’s orbit before announcing the plans last month. Joshua Kushner — the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — was considered a potential key investor in the proposal, sources told The Times of London.

Before Trump’s social media post on Monday, the White House distanced itself from the affair as concerns spread. Trump told reporters in early August that he had never spoken with Infantino about the plans.

Infantino reportedly sought private talks with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump as he faced growing pressure to resign, according to the New York Post and The Times. FIFA’s official media account said Infantino had not called Trump or members of his administration — calling it “pure fiction” — and a State Department spokesperson said Rubio and Infantino never spoke.

CONCACAF and UEFA, European soccer’s governing body, both rejected Infantino’s plan within days of its announcement — an objection that initially proved difficult for the FIFA president to work around. However, Mexico’s federation broke with the U.S., backing Infantino in a move that could potentially serve the country’s longer-term soccer interests. The country joined financial heavyweights like Qatar and the United Arab Emirates in support of the plan.

UEFA last week threatened Infantino, Joshua Kushner, JP Morgan and others involved with “legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints” over the doomed plans, The Telegraph reported. The letters warned against destroying or deleting any relevant documents ahead of potential legal action: “Given that proceedings are reasonably anticipated, you are obliged to preserve all relevant materials … with immediate effect.”

The European governing body had also said none of its teams would participate in future international matches unless they have assurances that Infantino will block FIFA competitions from private ownership. Unlike other global associations, UEFA has incredible leverage: It comprises a majority of top-seeded teams across the most recent men’s and women’s world cups, and the contests cannot realistically proceed without European participation, especially as the 2030 men’s tournament is scheduled to take place across stadiums in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

Others within the organization openly criticized Infantino’s proposal and its rollout, saying they were blindsided by the plans. Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino who sat on Trump’s White House World Cup Task Force, publicly resigned over the issue.
