entries.title: Civil Rights Groups Are Challenging Trump’s New ‘Birth Tourism’ Order
entries.summary: President Donald Trump “has apparently decided to keep trying” after the Supreme Court’s rejection of his last effort, the attorneys wrote.
entries.content:
The legal team that defended birthright citizenship in the Supreme Court is seeking to thwart President Donald Trump’s new effort to limit “birth tourism.”

In a filing Tuesday before the same federal district judge who blocked Trump’s previous birthright citizenship push, the attorneys requested a block against one of two new executive orders narrowing citizenship eligibility.

The filing argues that the Supreme Court ruling, which backed the longstanding 14th Amendment right of people born in the country to be granted U.S. citizenship, limited the exceptions of those who do not qualify and doesn’t give the president leeway for carving new exemptions.

“Faced with the Supreme Court’s rejection of his effort to rewrite the Citizenship Clause, the President has apparently decided to keep trying,” the attorneys for the American Civil Liberties Union and other civil rights groups wrote in the request for a preliminary injunction.

“If the President issues 100 orders seeking to create new exceptions to the sacred guarantee of the Citizenship Clause, all 100 will be equally illegal,” the attorneys wrote. “And nothing requires this Court to countenance the continued assault on this foundational constitutional principle or issue an endless string of EO-specific injunctions.”

The latest Trump executive orders follow his June loss in the Supreme Court, where he sought to exclude from citizenship children of undocumented immigrants or those with temporary authorization to be in the country.

“President Trump may not like the fact that birthright citizenship is a constitutional right, and he may not like that he lost in the Supreme Court, but that is really beside the point,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project and lead counsel. “It’s well past time for these illegal and cruel attacks on children’s citizenship to end.”

One of the new orders bars executive departments and agencies from issuing citizenship documents to people whose parents are deemed “alien enemies,” whose parents work for foreign governments or whose parents work for international organizations with immunity. It also attempts to deny citizenship when a parent “engaged in a commercial transaction” to guarantee being in the country at the time of birth.

Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who’s led the administration’s hard-line effort to restrict immigration, described the aim in the Oval Office.

“People come here, pretend to be a tourist, pretend to be a visitor — say they want to go to Disneyland, they want to go visit a monument or go to a national park, but the real reason they’re here is to have a child,” Miller said Thursday.

The executive order’s attempt to crack down on “birth tourism” is troublingly ambiguous, the filing states, pointing out that the lead plaintiff in the case, identified only as Barbara, bought a bus ticket on her journey to the U.S.

“The government’s vague new exception would thus set it up as the arbiter of which children deserve citizenship based on its assessment of their parents’ particular circumstances,” the attorneys wrote.

The ACLU, some of their state affiliates, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus, and Democracy Defenders Fund joined the filing.

Although the citizenship clause doesn’t grant the right to children of ambassadors and other representatives of foreign sovereigns, the attorneys argued the new executive order goes too far because it could also apply to staff at embassies who don’t have full diplomatic immunity, such as janitors and groundskeepers.

Another executive order Trump signed Thursday directs the state and homeland security secretaries to prevent immigrants from entering the country to give birth.

entries.title: Medical Groups Quickly Denounce Trump’s ‘Dangerous’ Vaccine Order
entries.summary: The influential organizations roundly criticized the order for the effects it could have on children’s health.
entries.content:
Numerous professional medical associations are openly opposing President Donald Trump’s executive order to reshape the nation’s childhood vaccine schedule, calling it a “dangerous” and abrupt departure from science-based recommendations.

The American Medical Association, American Academy of Pediatrics and American College of Physicians, among others, wrote in separate statements that the executive order is part of the second Trump administration’s amplification of vaccine skepticism. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s earlier attempts to change the vaccine schedule were blocked in court due to a legal challenge by the AAP.

The AAP said the order Trump signed Monday was “not only disheartening but dangerous.”

“There is no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance,” the group added in a statement Monday. “Dozens of studies involving millions of people show there is no link between vaccines and autism, and yet federal leaders continue to promote this outdated, disproven idea to scare families.”

Trump’s order calls for dividing childhood vaccines into three categories, with different recommendations for who should get them, and directs federal agencies to implement the changes. It also suggested splitting up combined vaccine doses, which are currently used to limit the number of hospital visits children must undergo, into separate shots.

The White House and conservative groups have clashed with the medical establishment over vaccine guidance since Trump returned to office.

In August 2025, eight medical groups announced in a joint statement that they were removed as liaison organizations to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices — a move that barred them from reviewing scientific evidence and providing vaccine recommendations. The federal government deemed the eight groups “biased” at the time of their removal, the joint statement said.

Trump has recently pressured Kennedy to move more aggressively on changing the childhood vaccine schedule and probing a repeatedly debunked link between vaccines and autism, according to news reports.

At Trump’s press conference Monday, the president made a slew of misleading and unsubstantiated claims — including that babies get “72 jabs,” a number that some fact-checkers have said might refer to the number of recommended vaccine doses that a child is eligible to receive before the age of 18.

“Nothing bad can happen from what we’re doing,” Trump said Monday. “Nothing bad can happen.”

Medical groups firmly disagreed.

Willie Underwood III, the president of the American Medical Association, one of the most influential medical groups in the country, said upending a “proven vaccination schedule without credible evidence risks” would weaken public confidence and put children’s health at risk.

The changes, if enacted, could also increase costs and place a “greater burden on families needing to schedule multiple appointments for a multiple-dose MMR vaccine,” said Jan Carney, president of the American College of Physicians.

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine wrote in a statement that “unnecessarily changing standard vaccinations” would negatively affect the health of mothers and children, and would “harm the health of families and communities.”

The World Health Organization, which Trump withdrew the United States from, shared a social media post Tuesday explaining why “timing matters for vaccines.” The National Foundation for Infectious Diseases and the Infectious Diseases Society of America also raised alarms that the changes were being proposed amid a resurgence of the measles.

“When vaccines become more difficult to obtain, fewer children are protected, increasing the risk that diseases long held in check can re-emerge,” NFID Medical Director Robert Hopkins said Monday. “At a time when communities across the country are confronting the return of preventable diseases, the nation should be strengthening its ability to protect children, not putting that progress at risk.”

entries.title: Trump Administration to End Federal Funding for Gender-Affirming Care for Children
entries.summary: “Please remember this when you are casting your vote,” President Trump said, tying the move to the upcoming midterm elections.
entries.content:
The Trump administration announced a new rule that would prevent federal Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program dollars from funding gender-affirming care for children after Oct. 13.

The rule, announced Tuesday, is part of a wider White House push to restrict transgender or nonbinary children from receiving gender-affirming procedures — particularly surgery, which is already a rare option for youth — and to more strictly define gender.

The rule blocks federal funding from going toward puberty blockers, gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery. It provides an exemption for treatments related to intersex conditions or complications from prior procedures.

The rule also carves out up to six months of funding for those already receiving gender-affirming hormone therapy after criticism rose during the public comment period. That funding is meant to allow beneficiaries “to phase off these medications in a manner that allows for clinical discretion.”

“Children deserve our protection, not experimental interventions that can have dangerous, lifelong consequences,” Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz said in a video announcing the rule.

“The government cannot keep signing these checks,” he continued, calling evidence for the procedures “weak.”

The rule bars funding for federal-state healthcare programs from going toward such gender-affirming care, but states can still help separately cover treatment costs. Over half of states have enacted laws limiting youth access to gender-affirming care, according to health policy organization KFF.

The agency projected a reduction in Medicaid and CHIP spending by $235 million over the next decade. More than $28 million of the roughly $31 million of Medicaid dollars spent on gender dysphoria treatment in 2023 went to hormone therapy or puberty blockers, the rule says, citing an analysis from that year. A little over $2.3 million went to inpatient or outpatient hospital services with surgery in the same time period.

Republicans at the state and federal level have moved to limit legal protections and health care access for transgender people while leaning heavily on the issue as a campaign message over the last two years. Trump on Tuesday applauded the agency’s announcement, reiterating his longstanding position against gender-affirming surgeries for children.

“Please remember this when you are casting your vote in the Midterm Elections in November,” he wrote on Truth Social.

A number of medical organizations, including the American Psychological Association, support wide access to psychological care and evidence-based treatment for transgender and nonbinary people.

Past White House efforts to curb gender-affirming care include Trump’s January 2025 order meant to cut off funding for similar treatments for people under 19, which prompted a lawsuit from Oregon, Washington state and New York.

Another coalition of states sued Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in December 2025 over an order that called gender-affirming treatments unsafe and ineffective and warned that doctors could be excluded from federal health programs for providing this care.

entries.title: Trump Administration Awards $158 Million Contract to Ex-ICE Official’s Nonprofit
entries.summary: The contract for legal services to unaccompanied minors went to Our Rescue, whose founder was the inspiration for the movie “Sound of Freedom.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration awarded a $158 million contract to a nonprofit to provide legal services for unaccompanied minors, a federal contracting database shows.

The Department of Health and Human Services awarded the one-year contract to Our Rescue, with a start date of Aug. 7 and the possibility of extension until Feb. 6, 2028. The grant was awarded by DHS’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, which oversees the care of unaccompanied undocumented children.

It’s unclear if Our Rescue has previously provided legal services to minors, and the group did not respond to a question from NOTUS about its legal experience. The group’s website does not list immigration litigation as a primary function.

It’s the second time this month that the Trump administration has awarded a contract for assisting minors in immigration cases to a firm outside of the advocacy groups that have previously handled such services.

Derek Benner, Our Rescue’s CEO, is a former ICE official. He told NOTUS in a statement that facilitating legal support to unaccompanied minors aligns with the organization’s mission.

“These are among the most vulnerable children in the world, and they deserve nothing less than the full weight of our experience,” Benner said. “We welcome this responsibility of working on their behalf.”

Tim Ballard, who founded Our Rescue in 2013, is a former ICE agent who was accused of sex trafficking and forced labor in lawsuits, which were later dismissed. The movie “Sound of Freedom” was inspired by his work supposedly combating sex trafficking.

Ballard abruptly resigned from the organization in 2023, shortly before the allegations were made public.

The federal government has allocated just over $158 million toward the contract, with a potential award amount of up to $244 million. It is the first award Our Rescue has landed with the federal government, per the federal contracting database.

The contract comes a little over a week after the federal government revealed plans to award a $150 million contract to Burke Law Group, a small Houston-based law firm, also to provide legal services to unaccompanied immigrant children.

The head of Burke Law Group, Marcella Burke, was a Trump appointee in his first administration. On Tuesday, HHS told Law360 that no grant had been finalized, but that it had “been in touch” with the firm.
